etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English preignant, from Old French preignant, pregnant, also prenant (compare archaic Modern French prégnant), and their source, Latin praegnāns (“pregnant”), probably from prae- (“pre-”) + *gnāscī, an archaic form of nāscī (“to be born”). Displaced Old English bearnēacen (literally "child-enlarged").

definitions.definition: Of a couple: expecting a baby together.
(chiefly not comparable) Carrying developing offspring within the body.

quote.citation: 2017 July 13, Bonnie Rochman, “Mothers-To-Be Aren’t Told Enough About Genetic Testing”, in Time‎[1]:
quote.text: Once upon a time, not so long ago, women got pregnant and spent nine months in suspense before finding out if they were having a boy or a girl. But today? That waiting game is completely outdated, even quaint.

definitions.definition: (comparable) Meaningful, having numerous possibilities or implications; full of promise; abounding in ability, resources, etc.

quote.citation: c. 1601–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Twelfe Night, or What You Will”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: wherein the pregnant enemy does much

quote.citation: 2019 January 26, Kitty Empire [pseudonym], “The Streets review – the agony and ecstasy of a great everyman”, in Katharine Viner, editor, The Guardian‎[2], London: Guardian News & Media, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 8 April 2019:
quote.text: The many tear-jerkers deal with finality, with death and the end of love, with a stoicism pregnant with feeling.

definitions.definition: (poetic) Fecund, fertile, prolific (usually of soil, ground, etc.).

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto VI”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: The sunne-beames bright vpon her body playd, / Being through former bathing mollifide, / And pierst into her wombe, where they embayd / With so sweet sence and secret power vnspide, / That in her pregnant flesh they shortly fructifide.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Affording entrance; receptive; yielding; willing; open; prompt.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iv]:
quote.text: play at subtill games; faire vertues all;To which the Grecians are most prompt and pregnant

quote.citation: 1843, William Robert Wilde, Austria: Its Literary, Scientific, and Medical Institutions:
quote.text: The Entbundenen, or those already delivered, are separate from those pregnants awaiting their accouchement

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Apparently from Middle French pregnant, preignant (“pressing, compelling”), present participle of prembre (“to press”), from Latin premere (“to press”).

quote.citation: 1751, [Tobias] Smollett, The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle […], volume (please specify |volume=I to IV), London: Harrison and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Peregrine was in a little time a distinguished character, not only for his acuteness of apprehension, but also for that mischievous fertility of fancy, of which we have already given such pregnant examples.
